steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper showing that ensembles of reward models combined with conservative optimization help mitigate overoptimization in RLHF. Explain the overoptimization problem, the synthetic gold-reward setup we build on (with label noise added), why ensembles beat scaling up the reward model, and list our contributions.

steps.text:

- Our study: ensembles + conservative optimization, setup with label noise
- Comparison with scaling the reward model
- Main contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- RLHF and overoptimization
  - RLHF: powerful technique to fine-tune/enhance LLM behaviors
  - fickle, many failure modes
  - overoptimization: progress on learned reward model, regress on true reward
  - anecdotal evidence in many RLHF works; only one prior work studies it systematically
  - that work: synthetic setup, human labelers expensive; much larger LM trained as "gold" reward model -> preference labels for proxy reward models
- Our study
  - systematic: do ensembles + conservative optimization mitigate overoptimization?
  - results: mitigates it and improves performance
  - setup identical to prior one, plus label noise
  - prior work assumes noise-free labels; real RLHF annotator agreement 60-75\%
  - add 25\% label noise; strong evidence in both no-noise and 25\% noise cases
- Scaling comparison
  - prior scaling laws: larger proxy reward model -> less overoptimization
  - but reward models come from pretrained LMs -> larger one needs significant, costly pretraining
  - ensembles: only fine-tune multiple copies of pretrained reward model, inexpensive
  - model and data scaling results (Figures 8 and 9): gains orthogonal to reward model size; combinable
- Contributions
  - first study of ensembles vs overoptimization in RLHF fine-tuning
  - BoN: ensembles + conservative optimization eliminate overoptimization, up to 70\% improvement in some cases
  - PPO: typically outperforms single reward model; with suitable KL penalty weight eliminates overoptimization
  - robustness to new hyperparameters (e.g. ensemble size)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
With large language models, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has become a powerful technique to fine-tune and enhance the behaviors of models. But even with its empirical success, RLHF is still a fickle method with many failure modes. One of these failure modes is overoptimization, where policy optimization seems to be making progress according to the learned reward model, but actually starts to regress with respect to the true reward function. Many works on RLHF have anecdotal evidence of overoptimization, but prior work is the only one that studies overoptimization systematically. Since working directly with human labelers is expensive, that work introduces a synthetic setup for studying overoptimization, where a much larger language model is first trained as a "gold" reward model and then used to generate preference labels to train proxy reward models.

In this work we do a systematic study of whether combining ensembles with conservative optimization can help mitigate overoptimization. Our results show that ensemble-based conservative optimization not only helps mitigate overoptimization, it also improves performance. Our setup is the same as that prior work's with one change, which is adding label noise. The prior work assumes the preference labels used to train the proxy reward model have no noise. But this does not mirror real-world RLHF, where agreement rates among human annotators are usually between 60-75\%. To simulate this disagreement and better reflect real-world RLHF, we also extend the setup to include 25\% label noise. In both cases, no label noise and 25\% label noise, we give strong evidence that ensemble-based conservative optimization methods work for mitigating overoptimization and improving performance.

- Scaling comparison
  - prior scaling laws: bigger proxy reward model -> less overoptimization
  - reward models from pretrained LMs; bigger needs costly pretraining, not always feasible
  - ensembles: fine-tune multiple copies of pretrained reward model, inexpensive
  - Figures 8 and 9: gains orthogonal to reward model size, can combine
- Contributions
  - first study of ensembles against overoptimization in RLHF
  - BoN: eliminates overoptimization, up to 70\% improvement in some cases
  - PPO: usually beats single reward model; with suitable KL penalty eliminates overoptimization
  - robustness to new hyperparameters (e.g. ensemble size)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
With large language models, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has become a powerful technique to fine-tune and enhance the behaviors of models. But even with its empirical success, RLHF is still a fickle method with many failure modes. One of these failure modes is overoptimization, where policy optimization seems to be making progress according to the learned reward model, but actually starts to regress with respect to the true reward function. Many works on RLHF have anecdotal evidence of overoptimization, but prior work is the only one that studies overoptimization systematically. Since working directly with human labelers is expensive, that work introduces a synthetic setup for studying overoptimization, where a much larger language model is first trained as a "gold" reward model and then used to generate preference labels to train proxy reward models.

In this work we do a systematic study of whether combining ensembles with conservative optimization can help mitigate overoptimization. Our results show that ensemble-based conservative optimization not only helps mitigate overoptimization, it also improves performance. Our setup is the same as that prior work's with one change, which is adding label noise. The prior work assumes the preference labels used to train the proxy reward model have no noise. But this does not mirror real-world RLHF, where agreement rates among human annotators are usually between 60-75\%. To simulate this disagreement and better reflect real-world RLHF, we also extend the setup to include 25\% label noise. In both cases, no label noise and 25\% label noise, we give strong evidence that ensemble-based conservative optimization methods work for mitigating overoptimization and improving performance.

The scaling laws for reward model overoptimization found by prior work show that increasing the size of the proxy reward model also reduces overoptimization. But reward models come from pretrained language models. So getting a larger reward model would need significant pretraining, which is not always feasible and can be very costly. Our approach with ensembles of reward models only needs fine-tuning of multiple copies of a reward model that is already pretrained, which is relatively inexpensive. Also, our model and data scaling results (Figures 8 and 9) show that the gains from our method are orthogonal to the gains from increasing reward model size, so the two approaches can be combined easily for even better results.

Our main contributions are:

- We do the first study of using ensembles to counter overoptimization in RLHF-based fine-tuning of language models.

- Our results show that using ensembles and conservative optimization eliminates overoptimization for BoN and gives up to 70\% improvement in some cases.

- For PPO, ensemble-based conservative optimization usually outperforms optimizing a single reward model, and when it is combined with a suitable KL penalty weight it eliminates overoptimization.

- We also do studies to establish that the ensemble-based conservative optimization methods are robust to the new hyperparameters they introduce (e.g. size of the ensemble).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
With the advent of large language models, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has emerged as a powerful technique to fine-tune and enhance models’ behaviors [1,2,3]. However, despite its empirical success, RLHF remains a fickle method that suffers from many failure modes [4]. One such failure mode is overoptimization, in which policy optimization appears to be making progress according to the learned reward model but in reality begins to regress with respect to the true reward function [1,5,6]. While many works on RLHF contain anecdotal evidence of overoptimization [1,5,7], [6] is the only work that studies overoptimization systematically. Since working directly with human labelers is expensive, [6] introduce a synthetic setup to study overoptimization, in which a much larger language model is first trained as a “gold” reward model and then used to generate preference labels for training proxy reward models.

In this work, we conduct a systematic study of whether combining ensembles with conservative optimization can help mitigate overoptimization. Our results indicate that ensemble-based conservative optimization not only helps mitigate overoptimization but also improves performance. Our setup is identical to that of [6] with one modification: the addition of label noise. [6] assume that the preference labels used to train the proxy reward model contain no noise. However, this does not mirror real-world RLHF, where agreement rates among human annotators are typically between 60-75\% [1,5,7]. To simulate this disagreement and better reflect real-world RLHF, we extend the setup to also include 25\% label noise. In both the no label noise and 25\% label noise cases, we provide strong evidence that ensemble-based conservative optimization methods are effective in mitigating overoptimization and improving performance.

The scaling laws for reward model overoptimization discovered by [6] indicate that increasing the size of the proxy reward model also reduces overoptimization. However, reward models are derived from pretrained language models, so acquiring a larger reward model would require significant pretraining, which is not always feasible and can be very costly [8,9]. Our approach, using ensembles of reward models, only requires fine-tuning multiple copies of an already pretrained reward model, which is relatively inexpensive. Moreover, our model and data scaling results (Figures 8 and 9) indicate that the gains from our method are orthogonal to those achieved by increasing reward model size; thus, the two approaches can be combined seamlessly for even better results.

Our main contributions are as follows:

- We conduct the first study of using ensembles to counter overoptimization in RLHF-based fine-tuning of language models.

- Our results indicate that using ensembles and conservative optimization eliminates overoptimization for BoN and yields up to 70\% improvement in some cases.

- For PPO, ensemble-based conservative optimization typically outperforms single reward model optimization and, when combined with a suitable KL penalty weight, successfully eliminates overoptimization.

- We further conduct studies establishing the robustness of the ensemble-based conservative optimization methods to the new hyperparameters they introduce (e.g. size of the ensemble).
